history.heading: The oldest republic
paragraphs: San Marino, a tiny country on the slopes of Mount Titano surrounded by Italy, claims to be the world's oldest surviving republic. According to tradition, it was founded in 301 CE by Marinus, a Christian stonemason from the island of Rab who fled persecution. Its statutes date from the 1600s, among the oldest constitutional documents still in force.

San Marino preserved its independence through the centuries thanks to its mountain fortress and diplomacy. Napoleon respected it, and during Italian unification it gave refuge to Giuseppe Garibaldi, and Italy agreed to respect its independence.

history.heading: Modern San Marino
paragraphs: San Marino stayed neutral in the Second World War, though it was bombed in 1944, and sheltered around 100,000 refugees. From 1945 to 1957 it had one of the first democratically elected communist governments in the world. It joined the Council of Europe in 1988 and the United Nations in 1992.

culture.heading: Traditions
paragraphs: Italian is the official language, and most people are Catholic. The historic centre and Mount Titano, with its three towers (Guaita, Cesta and Montale), are a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Torta Tre Monti, a layered wafer cake, is a local speciality. The Medieval Days festival recalls its history.

politics.heading: Two heads of state
paragraphs: San Marino has a unique system: two Captains Regent, elected by parliament every six months, serve jointly as heads of state, a tradition dating back to the 13th century. The 60-member Great and General Council is the parliament. San Marino is not an EU member but has negotiated an association agreement with the EU.

economy.heading: Small but wealthy
paragraphs: San Marino has a high income per person. Its economy relies on tourism, banking, manufacturing (ceramics, furniture and electronics) and selling stamps and coins to collectors. It uses the euro under an agreement with the EU.
